title: Early careers: Comparative design yields no findings
desc: Outlines age, pay, hiring and exposure comparisons but cannot establish AI displacement or legal staffing consequences.

kps.k: The cluster concerns whether AI exposure affects early-career employment differently from older workers, but the supplied extracts document comparisons rather than findings.
kps.d: Canaries in the Coal Mine compares headcount across exposure categories and age bands, including workers aged 22–25 and 26–30, with separate charts for computer occupations and software developers. These designs address age-specific labour-market effects; the extracted labels do not reveal trend directions, effect sizes or causal displacement. The supplied material therefore neither establishes nor refutes disproportionate harm to entry-level workers.

kps.k: The analysis separates employment changes from real-pay adjustment and distinguishes existing employees from new hires.
kps.d: Canaries examines annual base compensation by age, occupation and exposure, adjusted to 2017 dollars using the PCE deflator. Its August 2026 revision separately examines job-stayers and newly hired workers; the job-stayer chart uses a November 2022 index and displays dates through July 2026. These distinctions allow different channels of adjustment to be examined, but the supplied extracts show neither wage gains nor wage losses.

kps.k: Exposure definitions and sample choices qualify what the employment comparisons can establish.
kps.d: The August 2026 Canaries revision uses distinct measures: Eloundou et al.'s GPT-4 β exposure, Anthropic Economic Index augmentative exposure and Felten et al.'s image-generation exposure. These measures should not be treated as interchangeable evidence of automation. Sample variants include part-time and temporary workers and exclude technology firms; the unqualified version also identifies a men-only sample. The exclusions differ across versions: NAICS 51 in the unqualified extracts versus 51 and 5415 in the revision. Captions identify these checks but do not establish that results survive them.

kps.k: The supplied evidence cannot resolve disagreement about AI's labour-market effects or justify legal-sector staffing conclusions.
kps.d: The August 2026 Canaries revision offers annual ACS comparisons for 2021–2024 and references monthly CPS counterparts, but the extracts do not show whether those surveys corroborate one another. The supplied material from Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects, revised as Still Waters, Rapid Currents, contains only figure fragments, including legal-professional panels. Neither its title nor those panels establish a counter-finding. Practical interpretation requires readable estimates, version-specific periods and sector-specific evidence before drawing conclusions about junior-lawyer displacement or changing recruitment.

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research sources support the proposition that these extracts describe comparative designs but do not provide recoverable findings about AI displacement or legal-sector staffing. Across the material, the common basis is evidentiary limitation: captions and labels identify comparisons by age, occupational group, AI-exposure measure, employment, and real compensation, but do not preserve readable trends, effect sizes, regression estimates, or causal conclusions. Material variation concerns methodological scope rather than substantive position. Some fragments contain almost no recoverable content; the Canaries extracts document age and exposure comparisons plus sample variants; and the August 2026 revision adds separate analysis of job-stayers and new hires, multiple exposure measures, technology-firm exclusions, and ACS/CPS comparisons. These refinements show a more developed research design but still do not establish whether early-career workers were harmed, whether any association was caused by AI, or whether the results apply to junior lawyers. This assessment concerns only the curated sources supplied, not academia or researchers generally.

elens.an: The 2025 materials support the cluster’s principal proposition that the supplied extracts identify comparative designs but yield no recoverable findings about AI displacement or legal staffing consequences. Across these curated sources, the available evidence consists chiefly of figure labels, age bands, exposure categories, compensation definitions and sample variants; it does not preserve readable trend directions, effect sizes or causal estimates. The Canaries extracts show that the study compares early-career workers aged 22–25 and 26–30 with older groups, separates exposure categories, examines real compensation and varies sample definitions. However, those methodological details cannot establish whether employment or pay rose or fell. Internal variation concerns the amount and type of recoverable design information: one record contains only fragmented occupational panels, including legal professionals, while the Canaries records provide more specific age, exposure, pay and sample labels. Neither supplies sector-specific results capable of supporting conclusions about junior-lawyer recruitment or displacement.

elens.an: The August 2026 revision supports the proposition that the supplied material establishes a comparative research design but not substantive findings. It disaggregates workers by age and AI exposure, separates employment from real-pay adjustment, distinguishes job-stayers from new hires, and references robustness checks and occupation-level regressions. However, the supplied excerpts provide no readable estimates, effect sizes, trend directions or causal results, so they cannot establish disproportionate displacement of early-career workers or justify conclusions about legal-sector staffing. Internal variation lies in the study’s methods—different exposure measures, worker groups, pay margins, samples and survey sources—not in competing substantive conclusions visible in the extracts.
